extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, students/scholars of public administration and constitutional design, senior civil servants
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for structuring and staffing executive departments under a parliamentary system, and for selecting and evaluating ministers and permanent officials. Includes comparisons with other forms of government and practical guidance on office composition and recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of generalist leading minds at the top
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading minds who generalise and act upon various materials are useful only if they occupy the top positions: 'They must not be at the bottom--they must not even be half way up--they must be at the top.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such leaders combine specialties, clarify boundaries between roles, and add wide knowledge of large affairs that specialists lack. Example/analogy: the merchant (generalist) can advise across institutions where clerks cannot. Anti-pattern: putting generalists in low positions where they cannot exercise overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic (outsider) head as corrective of bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrusion from without upon an office of an exterior head is essential to prevent the office becoming technical, self-absorbed, and self-multiplying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Parliamentary head can question whether procedures 'conduce to the end in view' and remove obsolete formalities. Junior clerks asking such questions would be 'pooh-poohed'; only the head can get them answered. Use the head to bring 'the rubbish of office to the burning-glass of sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Minister's proper function: ensure the department is properly worked
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'not the business of a Cabinet Minister to work his department. His business is to see that it is properly worked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a minister does the department's work personally he probably does harm; permanent staff can do routine work better. Ministers should be keen critics and rational correctors rather than day-to-day operators. Example: Sir George Lewis as model Parliamentary head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minister as animator: rousing departments to perceive public needs
rubrics_metrics.description: A fresh mind applied to the official mind is also an animating use: ministers can rouse departments to duties the vague public perceives before the administration does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Duke of Newcastle roused up his department during the Crimean War (though it could not act when roused). Ministers should supply animating capacity in addition to critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent change of Parliamentary minister is advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent change in the official is an advantage because no single individual can perfectly represent outside sense or exercise both impelling power and restraining wisdom; long contact with an office will destroy the minister's outsider utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotating ministers prevents acclimatisation to office ways ('the dyer's hand would be subdued to what it works in'). Use change to mix different talents (impulse vs restraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary scrutiny reveals incompetence
rubrics_metrics.description: A considerable Cabinet Minister must publicly defend his department; public exposure in Parliament will quickly show substantial incompetence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ministers must explain and argue publicly, fools are soon discovered; parliamentary government provides an effective procedure for testing ministers' competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholesale turnover of officials (preserve a permanent skilled bureaucracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Presidential system that changes the whole official class with each administration is incompatible with a skilled bureaucracy because it enables patronage and prevents continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In systems where officials change en masse, patronage becomes pervasive ('bribery') and administrative skill erodes. Contrast with parliamentary systems where individual MPs cannot promise places as effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks and trade-offs of other government forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary and dictatorial forms have distinct pros/cons: hereditary selection risks whim and incompetence; dictatorial selection can yield very able administrators but at the cost of instability, fear, and catastrophic interregna.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictators may select excellent administrators due to personal stakes, but this efficiency comes 'at a price altogether transcending its value' — threats to property, interregna of incapacity, and regime violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate administrative performance relative to scope attempted
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms of administrative inefficiency must account for the scale and difficulty of what is attempted (e.g., defending a scattered empire vs continental states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons with other nations should consider differing tasks and constraints (volunteer vs conscript armies, global vs continental responsibilities); apparent inefficiency may reflect larger or harder assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local independence vs central action
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of local authority affects the central executive's ability to act; local independence can hinder central action when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of independent local authorities (e.g., metropolitan local bodies) may prevent the central government from acting effectively, but the appropriate degree of local freedom depends on national circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ignorance and national culture limit government effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: No polity can get out of a nation more than there is in the nation; a free government depends on persuasion, so popular ignorance or lack of culture degrades policy quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: weak foreign policy traced to insular minds, lack of education about modern world. Improving public/business education is necessary to raise administrative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service must be attractive to recruit ability
rubrics_metrics.description: If Government service is not socially or economically attractive, the best men will not go into the public bureaucracy, reducing administrative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some countries government posts are coveted and attract elites; in England at the time, public offices could not buy the best ability with 'pure honour' and mercantile opportunities drew talented minds away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized, coherent design of administrative system matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrations that were arranged deliberately by a designing genius (e.g., Napoleon, Frederick the Great) produced more effective, consistent, and enduring systems than those that grew casually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English offices 'grew as each could' and exhibit unsystematic duties and anomalous responsibilities; a coherent stage-wide design improves administrative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offices should have clear, reasoned alignment of duties and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties ought to be assigned for administrative reasons that make sense in future governance, not merely for historical accident; titles should reflect real responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: First Lord of Treasury having little to do with Treasury; 'Woods and Forests' looking after sewerage; responsibilities lodged under distant judges or historical sinecures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform and reasoned machinery for presenting business to the minister
rubrics_metrics.description: Where business is similar, the machinery for bringing it before the extrinsic chief ought largely to be similar; yet in practice no two offices had exactly alike relations between permanent officials and the Parliamentary chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistency between offices (Army vs Navy vs Board of Trade vs Treasury) creates confusion. Offices should be designed so ministers receive comparable, reasoned advice and information across departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a single permanent responsible head in large departments
rubrics_metrics.description: In great administrative departments there ought to be some one permanent responsible head through whom the changing Parliamentary chief always acts and learns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example of the Exchequer suggests a responsible head improves continuity; for very large, complex departments (Admiralty, Home Office) a single principal head is often essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer competent, responsible secretaries over unwieldy boards
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Council of a Cabinet Minister is a number of highly paid, much occupied, responsible secretaries whom the Minister can consult; boards may conceal incompetence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. James Wilson's view: a permanent under-secretary charged with control must be able or the Minister will be blamed. A board member may be incompetent and do nothing, whereas a close secretary cannot be chosen negligently without political cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should consult the ablest, most responsible advisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers (e.g., the Chancellor of the Exchequer) succeed when they take the opinions, oral or written, of the ablest and most responsible persons in relevant offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gladstone acknowledged dependence on skilled advisers in Ways and Means; this practice produced 'the best budget in the world.' Apply same method to other departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain separation between judicial office and administrative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is contrary to principle that any part of administration should be entrusted to a judge; administration of justice should be kept clear of sinister temptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: the Lord Chancellor holding administrative duties while being a judge and Cabinet minister leads to anomalies and conflicts of interest (e.g., making party speeches while deciding cases).
